881.quote_or_event: “What is this evil whim of warriors for persistence in heroism in which there is such a quarrel between brothers ending in destruction? If my elder brother does not live, enough of life for me.”
881.explanation: In Hemacandra's telling, Bāhubali has just felled his elder brother Bharata in their duel over the kingdom, and he fans the unconscious man with his garment, weeping, appalled at what the quarrel has made of two sons of Ṛṣabha.
881.tie_back: The Kural warns that kin, like shade and water, are a comfort that turns to pain once they turn harmful, and the duel of Bharata and Bāhubali is the classic Jain case of brothers whose closeness became the source of their deepest injury.
881.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1 (Ādīśvara-caritra), ch. 5, part 11 'The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)
881._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Johnson's translation on wisdomlib.org. The brothers' strife fits the theme of kin turned harmful, but the Kural's shade-and-water simile has no counterpart, and the Jain story ends in Bāhubali's renunciation rather than ruin.

882.quote_or_event: “A little monkey breaking into a fruit with its finger, will strike and seize its own father … the friendship of those who are without unity (of mind) is not pleasant.”
882.explanation: The Jain-authored Tamil Nāladiyār, in its chapter on improper friendship, pictures the young monkey that turns on its own father as he comes to meet it, and says that closeness without real unity of mind brings no pleasure.
882.tie_back: The Kural tells us to fear the foe who comes in the guise of kin more than the open swordsman, and the quatrain's monkey striking the father who comes to greet it is exactly that danger inside an intimate bond.
882.source: Nāladiyār 24.7 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
882._accuracy_note: Checked against the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib.org; an ellipsis marks the omitted words 'thongh coming to meet it. Lord of the hills!'. This is Tamil Jain literature, not canonical scripture, and it warns against hollow intimacy without the Kural's explicit sword-versus-kinsman contrast.

883.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
883.explanation: Asked by Keśi how he withstands the thousands of foes that attack him, Gautama names the true enemies as the unsubdued self, the four passions and the five senses, all of them inside the person.
883.tie_back: The Kural urges a man to fear the enemy within and guard himself, and Gautama's answer turns the same vigilance on the foes that live inside one's own camp.
883.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
883._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The inward-enemy idea is a strong thematic fit; the Jain text spiritualises what the Kural treats as hidden enmity within one's household or court.

884.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
884.explanation: The Saman Suttam, gathering canonical Jain verses, names how each of the four passions (kaṣāyas) unravels a particular bond: anger kills affection and deceit kills friendship.
884.tie_back: The Kural says that when hidden enmity takes root in an unreformed mind it turns one's own people against one, and the Jain verse shows how the untamed passions of such a mind destroy love and friendship.
884.source: Saman Suttam 135 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
884._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com's Saman Suttam (Samyamasūtra). Good fit for an unreformed mind wrecking relationships; the verse speaks of the passions in general rather than of enmity among kin.

885.quote_or_event: “When Marbhuti, out of love for his brother, went to bring Kamatha back, the wretched fellow hurled a stone slab on his brother Marubhuti; consequently he died then and there”
885.explanation: In the Jain account of Pārśvanātha's former lives, Kamaṭha's hatred for his brother Marubhūti did not end with that murder: across later births he kept tormenting the soul that would become Pārśva, while Marubhūti's soul kept forgiving.
885.tie_back: The Kural warns that enmity born within the bond of kinship brings evils of a deadly kind, and Kamaṭha's fratricide, renewed birth after birth, is Jainism's best-known picture of exactly that.
885.source: Story of Kamaṭha and Marubhūti (previous lives of Pārśvanātha), as retold on Jain Square, 'Kamatha and Marabhuti' (jainsquare.wordpress.com)
885._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on the Jain Square page, a devotional web retelling (web tier); the spelling 'Marbhuti' is the site's. The story itself belongs to the Pārśvanātha narratives such as Hemacandra's Triṣaṣṭi, which I did not check in this session. Very close in theme: kin enmity that ends in death.

886.quote_or_event: “But when Mahavira refused to admit his claim, Jamali felt humiliated and finally left him to establish his own order. His order, however, does not appear to have lasted for long.”
886.explanation: Jamāli, a monk of Mahāvīra's own order and by tradition his kinsman, caused the first schism (nihnava). His following fell away, and the breakaway group did not survive him.
886.tie_back: The Kural says that once discord arises among those who were united, escaping ruin is hard, and the first Jain schism shows a split from within a united community ending in the dissenter's own decline.
886.source: Jain community history, 'Rival Sects' (Nihnavas section), jainworld.com
886._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on the jainworld.com page (secondary historical summary, not scripture). The ruin falls on the faction that broke away, not on the whole community, so the match is partial.

887.quote_or_event: “He started as a pupil and ended as a frustrated rival of Mahavira.”
887.explanation: Gośāla lived and wandered with Mahāvīra for six years as a self-declared disciple, then broke away, founded the Ājīvika order, and finally attacked Mahāvīra and two of his monks with his fiery power (tejolesyā).
887.tie_back: The Kural's casket and lid look like one object without being one, and Gośāla's six years at Mahāvīra's side, outwardly together but never one in mind, ending in open attack, illustrate that false union.
887.source: T.U. Mehta, The Path of Arhat, 'Association with Gosala' (jainworld.com)
887._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com (secondary account based on the Bhagavatī Sūtra). Strong fit for a union that only looks whole, though Gośāla is a disciple rather than a member of a family or clan.

888.quote_or_event: “Even one who has subsided or repressed all his passions, once more experiences a terrible spiritual degeneration, hence one ought not to become complacent when some remnants of passions still continue.”
888.explanation: Jain teaching warns that passions which have only been suppressed, not destroyed, keep working on the soul and can bring about a steep fall from spiritual heights already reached.
888.tie_back: The Kural pictures a family worn down by internal enmity as metal ground away by a file, and the Jain verse likewise describes a hidden remnant that keeps wearing away what has been won.
888.source: Saman Suttam 133 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
888._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. Next-best match only: it shares the idea of a lingering inner force that slowly erodes, but it concerns the individual soul, not a family, and has no image of a file.

889.quote_or_event: “One should not be complacent with a small debt, slight wound, spark of fire and slight passion, because what is small (today) may become bigger (later).”
889.explanation: This well-known Jain maxim sets a small passion beside a small debt, wound and spark: none of them may be trusted to stay small.
889.tie_back: The Kural says that enmity within, even as slight as half a sesame seed, holds ruin inside it, and the Jain maxim makes the same point that a trifling inner fault must never be dismissed.
889.source: Saman Suttam 134 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
889._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. A close match on 'small but fatal'; the Jain verse speaks of passion in general rather than enmity among one's own people.

890.quote_or_event: “For those who are wise, to become companions of the wicked is like the nâgâ playing with the female cobra.”
890.explanation: The closing quatrain of the Nāladiyār's chapter on improper friendship says that for a wise person, keeping close company with the wicked is as dangerous as sporting with a cobra.
890.tie_back: The Kural likens living with those who do not share one's mind to sharing a small hut with a snake, and the Jain Tamil quatrain uses the same serpent image for intimacy with the ill-disposed.
890.source: Nāladiyār 24.10 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
890._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib.org. Tamil Jain literature, not canonical scripture; the snake image matches closely, but the quatrain warns against the wicked in general rather than unreconciled housemates.
